DISTRICT AND ASSOCIATION DESCRIPTIONS
The Little Lake City School District (District or Management) is a suburban elementary school
district located in the southeastern portion of Los Angeles County. The District lies within the
municipalities of Santa Fe Springs, Norwalk, and Downey. The nine schools, seven elementary
and two middle, serve a diverse student population of 3,396. The ethnic distribution of the
student body is approximately 90% Hispanic, 2.8% White/non-Hispanic, 1.4% African-
American, and approximately 6% other. English learners account for 8.1% of the student
population, and 66.5% of English learners identify their primary language as Spanish.
Approximately 79% of students districtwide qualify for free/reduced lunch. All nine schools
receive federal Title I, and state Local Control Funds (including supplemental and concentration
funds for English learners, socioeconomically disadvantaged, and foster students). The District
offers a full-day transitional kindergarten and kindergarten program at all seven elementary sites.
An emphasis on learning, collaboration, and results is reflected in many of the practices at all
sites.
Little Lake Education Association (LLEA or Union) was established in December 1976. It is the
union representing 199 members, including general education and special education classroom
teachers, teachers on special assignment (TOSAs), one school nurse, one speech language
pathologist, and one adapted PE teacher.
LLEA operates as a local union chapter affiliated with the California Teachers Association
(CTA) and the National Education Association (NEA). Through these affiliations, the
association participates in statewide efforts to advocate for public education, educators, and
students.
HISTORY OF NEGOTIATIONS
The parties “sunshined” their respective proposals to the public on May 7, 2025 and May , and
met for four sessions from September 2025 through October 2025. PERB certified an impasse
and a mediator from the State Medication and Conciliation Service was assigned. The parties
had five mediation sessions from January 14 through February 20, 2026. The mediator certified
the parties to fact finding on February 23, 2026.
FACTFINDING CRITERIA
Pursuant to California Government Code Section 3548.2, the panel has considered and been
guided by the following statutory criteria:
1. State and federal laws that are applicable to the Employer.
2. Stipulations of the parties.
3. The interests and welfare of the public and the financial ability of the public
schools.
4. Comparison of the wages, hours, and conditions of employment of the employees
involved in the fact-finding proceeding with the wages, hours, and conditions of
2

employment of other employees performing similar services and with other
employees generally in public school employment in comparable communities.
5. The Consumer Price Index for goods and services, commonly known as the cost of
living.
6. The overall compensation presently received by the employees, including direct
wage compensation, vacations, holidays, and other excused time, insurance and
pensions, medical and hospitalization benefits, the continuity and stability of
employment, and all other benefits received.
7. Such other facts not confined to those specified in paragraphs 1 through 6,
inclusive, which are normally and traditionally taken into consideration in making
such findings and recommendations.
ISSUES BEFORE THE PANEL
There are five Articles before the Panel:
• Article XII – Class Size
• Article XIX – Hours of Employment
• Article XVII– Miscellaneous
• Article XX – Compensation
• Article XXI – Health and Welfare Benefits
Chair’s note: The parties have reached verbal consensus on some of the provisions under some
of these Articles. The Chair will focus the attention on the outstanding provisions presented at
the Hearing and will assume the parties will incorporate those verbal agreements within the
appropriate Articles when agreement on the entire collective bargaining agreement is reached.
The Chair’s Findings and Recommendations
The parties find themselves in a dilemma around Health and Welfare benefits. For
approximately the past 20 years, the District and the Association have entered into a series of
agreements that used one-time funding to provide additional employer contributions to the
District cap contributions established in the parties Collective Bargaining Agreement (“CBA”).
Those negotiated additional contributions provided full benefit coverages with no out-of-pocket
monthly employee contributions. Unfortunately, the benefit “caps” remained in the contract and
were not adjusted upwards as benefit costs increased. This plan year, beginning January 1, 2026,
the District chose to enforce the caps contained within the CBA without supplementing the costs
with any kind of funding, one-time or ongoing, and employees found themselves from paying $0
out-of-pocket to in some cases paying almost $1,400 per month (Kaiser with family option).
This decision to cease relying on one-time funding to ignore addressing the real benefit cap in
the CBA has soured the relationship and effects all aspects of this reopened negotiations. The
3

Chair’s recommendations on all Articles will center around establishing permanent, on-going
funding to Health and Welfare Benefits and cease the use of one-time funding for this purpose.
After a review of the facts and arguments presented by both parties, the Chair recommends the
following for each of the Articles before the panel:
Term (Combination of Article I and Article V)
The Parties have been negotiating for eleven months and the tone of bargaining has turned
contentious. Although they reached impasse on the last year, 2025-2026, of a three year
agreement, the Chair believes the parties would benefit from being away from the bargaining
table instead of immediately reopening the successor year, 2026-2027. The Chair is firm in his
belief that an agreement is preferable to a job action and a “locked-down” contract through 2026-
2027 would benefit both sides. It will also give clear predictability for personal budgets for the
union members and for District budget planning for 2026-27
Recommendation 1: Term – The Chair recommends the parties close 2025-2026 and
enter into a 3 year Agreement from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2029. All Articles
would be closed for 2026-2027 and 2027-2028 will have reopeners on all Compensation
(Articles XX and XI) with three additional Articles per side. Additionally, for 2027-
2028, each party could propose a new Article on Special Education. Reopeners for 2028-
2029 will be all Compensation (Articles XX and XI) with three additional Articles per
side.
Article XII – Class Size
From the materials provided by each side and the Union’s presentation, it appears to the Chair
that the District has not staffed class sizes to the levels contained the CBA. The District
estimates that between retirements and possible reductions in force (RIFs) there is a possibility
that nine unit members will not be replaced in 2026-2027, thereby effecting class sizes as well as
relieving the budget commitment of almost $1 million. This would be a key source of ongoing
funding.
The District has proposed these additional increases to class size for 2026-2027 and 2027-2028:
2026-2027
• TK-3 increase average class size to 27:1, with Kindergarten classes capped at 27
• 4-6 staffing ratios at 1:33
• 7-8 Staffing ratios at 1:30
2026-2027
• TK-3 increase average class size to 27:1, with Kindergarten classes capped at 27
• 4-6 staffing ratios at 1:33
• 7-8 Staffing ratios at 1:30
4

The Association proposes Status Quo on the Class Size Article
From the data, the Chair believes the District has not staffed to the limits within this Article but
does agree that raising and staffing to the limits would result in fewer staff generating more
available ongoing funding. The proposed TK-3 numbers would increase the average by 3
immediately, which may be too large in increase in one year.
Recommendation 2: Class Size - The Chair recommends the following adjustments:
2026-2027
• TK-3 Status Quo
• 4-6 staffing ratios at 1:33
• 7-8 Staffing ratios at 1:30
2027-2028
• TK-3 increase average class size to 27:1, with Kindergarten classes capped at 27
• 4-6 staffing ratios at 1:33
• 7-8 Staffing ratios at 1:30
Article XXI – Health and Welfare Benefits
Health Benefit premium are calculated for the calendar year, January 1 through December 31,
which will span two fiscal years. Out of pocket employee contributions are paid tenthly, but the
District must pay the premiums twelfthly. This calculation often confuses people. The Chair
will use the annual premium (which again is the calendar year and spans two fiscal years) for his
recommendation.
The Chair’s recommendation must attempt to address ongoing funding for Health and Welfare
benefits while keeping in mind the District’s budget. Also, the days of low class size and fully
provided benefits with no out of pocket may be over for the foreseeable future with the
forecasted state funding. Using the approximate million dollars generated from the decrease in
staff to provide on-going funding, the Chair makes the following recommendation.
Recommendation 3: Health and Welfare Benefits
New language in the CBA will have the District funding the Blue Shield Access Plus at
85% of premium at all tiers (ee, ee+1, ee+2 or more) with the employee paying 15% out-
of-pocket. The amount of 85% of Blue Shield Access Plus will be the “cap” spent on
every other plan at all tiers. Should the choice of plans change, the parties will reach
agreement on a new base plan as nearest to cost as Blue Shield Access Plus.
Article XX – Compensation (Salary)
Recognizing the priority of funding Health and Welfare, neither side proposed any ongoing
adjustment to the schedule.
5

Both side acknowledge the need for recruiting and retaining Speech and Language Pathologists
(SLP), both sides exchanged proposals for a new schedule to help recruit and retain SLPs to
eliminate the more expensive option of contracting out. The Chair recommends the District’s
position for a new Speech and Language Pathologist Salary Schedule.
Two other items are in this category of Compensation. It appears that the parties have a mutual
interest in compensating 5th grade teachers attending Science Camp with a one-time $500
stipend. It also appears that the parties have a mutual interest in compensating SDC
mild/moderate elementary teachers assigned to a combination classroom of three or more grade
levels shall be paid an annual stipend of $1,000 and moderate/severe elementary teachers
assigned to a combination classroom of four or more grade levels shall be paid an annual stipend
of $1,000.
Recommendation 4: Compensation
• No change to the salary schedule for 2025-2026
• Adopt Speech and Language Pathologist Salary Schedule as proposed by the
District (Attachment #1)
• $500 stipend for 5th grade teachers attending Science Camp
• $1000 annual stipend for SDC mild/moderate elementary teachers assigned to a
combination classroom of three or more grade levels
• $1000 annual stipend for moderate/severe elementary teachers assigned to a
combination classroom of four or more grade levels
Article XIX – Hours of Employment
Again, there may be some consensus regarding some provisions in this section, but the
outstanding issue seemed to be completing annual training during the first week of school. The
District wishes that the teachers complete that annual training during one of the minimum days
of that first week and the Association proposes it not be done during preparation time. It seems
the parties agree to increase the first week of school from 3 minimum days to as many as 5
minimum days. It seems obvious to the Chair that this required training be completed sometime
during that first week and the District proposal does not seem to be onerous, especially if the first
week of minimum days have increased.
Recommendation 5: Hours
Teachers to complete the required annual training during the first week of school and
the site administrator be charged with managing the timing of that training.
Article XVII – Miscellaneous
Candidly, the Chair was somewhat at a loss with this seemingly catch-all Article, appropriately
named “Miscellaneous”. There were over a dozen and a half seemingly unrelated items in this
that, frankly seem too much of a stretch of effort to resolve each one. A number of these issues
6

were new and related to Special Education and seemed unrelated to other items in this Article.
The Chair will leave it to the parties to resolve this category of “Miscellaneous” as much better
prepared to understand each of the nuances and discussions that preceded the impasse.
However, since a number of these provisions do seem to revolve around Special Education, the
Chair feels it appropriate to address how the parties can move forward on items regarding
Special Education. Included in the material the Association presented at the Hearing, was a
March 5, 2005 document titled, “Special Education Study” completed by Bridge 2 Inclusive
Practices. This over 100 page document is a study of the Little Lake City School District with,
the Chair assumes, an overall assessment of current services and recommendations regarding its
Special Ed program.
Several of the proposed changes under this “Miscellaneous” Article likely originated from this
study. The Chair is not an expert in Special Education and does not feel confident making
recommendations regarding specific programs or the personnel who provide these services to
students. However, the Chair does have knowledge of best practices in labor-management
collaboration to address such issues.
The Chair strongly believes that a joint committee, task force, or recommending body composed
of experienced district practitioners and managers would be best equipped to develop informed
recommendations based on this study. Engaging the individuals most directly affected by
potential changes—alongside program managers—in a collaborative process is far more likely to
result in meaningful and positive outcomes than proposals exchanged solely across the
negotiations table. Additionally, the Chair believes the parties would benefit from moving away
from confrontational negotiations to a process of dialogue and problem solving. The parties
could place any recommendations in a new Article of the CBA titled “Special Education” or
embed them within existing Articles of the CBA (not “Miscellaneous”).
Recommendation 6: Miscellaneous
The Chair recommends the formation of a Special Education Task Force with the
following:
• An equal number of participants from the Association and the Administration
• Joint co-chairs
• The charge of this Task Force is to implementing recommendations from the
expert report and, with fidelity, address concerns raised within district programs
• Use consensus decision-making after being trained in Interest Based Problem
Solving.

Dissenting In Part Report of Panel Member Su
PERB CASE NO: LA-IM-4206-E
Little Lake City School District and Little Lake Education Association
Su, Panel Member for the union, dissenting in part:
Health and Welfare Benefits
Although I agree that the main item at issue between the parties is health benefits, the supposed use of
one-time funds to provide employer contributions above the 2015 cap is an example of a clear lack of
the District prioritizing employee compensation in the form of health benefits which is an expense that
is reasonably predictable year-over-year and a benefit necessary to attract and retain qualified
employees. The Union’s analysis of the LLCSD’s finances demonstrates how LLCSD can prioritize
employee educator health and welfare benefits in its budget. LLCSD has an increasing trend of
spending more each year on outside contractors for positions that should be filled by employees who
are in the best position to meet the needs of students. Adjusting this pattern and actually budgeting
increases to revenue that have already been articulated by the Governor’s January State Budget
Proposal will provide sufficient funding to meet LLEAs health benefits demands without the need to
increase class sizes in 2026-27. The District should have sufficient time to convert contracted positions
in the 2026-27 school year to employees, and given the 15 layoff notices already issued, the District
may already have the staff to fill those positions.
I commend the chair’s efforts in recommending the Blue Shield Access Plus plan as the basis of an
ongoing premium sharing arrangement. However, 85%/15% is too high an out of pocket premium
contribution per month (employee $165, $ employee + 1 $330, family $430; Kaiser employee $227, $
employee + 1 $498, family $589) and I would suggest a 90%/10% split as a more reasonable
compromise moving down from 100% paid coverage that has been the standard in the district for
decades. This would align them with comparable districts. At the high out-of-pocket premiums LLEA
educators are currently paying for Blue Shield Access Plus (employee $410, employee + 1 $819,
family $1,065), LLCSD is ranked lower than all neighboring districts for healthcare contributions.
High out-of-pocket healthcare premiums coupled with a zero salary increase in 2025-26, the District
can expect to lose educators to districts with better compensation.
I concur that the implementation of whatever the parties agree to in the way of health benefits should
be ongoing and retroactive to January 2026, to provide some relief for the very extreme out-of-pocket
costs educators are enduring now.
Compensation
Although the LLCSD’s certificated salary compensation ranks poorly, the union chose, for 2025-26 to
prioritize fully paid health benefits, therefore I concur with the chair’s recommendation for no change
in the salary schedule for 2025-26. In addition, the remaining compensation recommendations are also
appropriate.
Class Size
It is important to note that class size was not even an issue on the table for most of the pre-impasse
negotiations and was a late sunshine by the District and only proposed as part of a package deal that
1

the Union rejected. Therefore, they have had little actual discussion about how these changes would
impact educator working conditions, student learning conditions, and the estimated value of the
savings that the District would achieve by worsening those conditions.
I concur with the chair that the District should certainly staff to the class size ratios and caps that are
already in the CBA before demanding higher class sizes. I also agree that with the current layoffs and
natural attrition, the District will save more than $1 million dollars in 2026-27 which should absolutely
be used to support the costs of employee health benefits moving forward.
As a practical matter, it is unlikely that the District would be able to implement any further changes to
class size in the 2026-27 year unless there is an unexpected exodus of teachers before the start of next
year as they have indicated that the current layoffs and anticipated retirements would only allow them
to staff to the current CBA. Therefore, there is no point in agreeing to higher class sizes for 2026-27
and it is not appropriate to tie up the agreement beyond 2026-27 (see comments on Term below).
Hours of Employment
I concur that the parties had some conceptual agreement on having minimum days the first week of
instruction for 2026-27. I would like to expand on the chair’s recommendation to clarify that this
online training be done post student dismissal on the two days that are already allotted to site
administrator discretion.
Term
The year at impasse is 2025-26 and given how late we are in the academic year, a two year term, 2025-
27 is reasonable. The Association intends to negotiate a successor agreement after that and should be
afforded the right to do so since 2026-27 would be the year for a successor agreement given the term
of the current CBA.
Miscellaneous
The chair has recommended the formation of a Special Education Task Force ostensibly to implement
the recommendations from the expert report which I concur that said special education report
recommendations should be implemented. Until such time as the parties can bargain for a Special
Education article, there are a few items that should be adopted as a part of this CBA.
SDC
Based on the recommended caseloads for certain SDC classes in the expert special education report, if
the caseloads below are exceeded, the teacher shall receive $350 per month that their caseload is
exceeded.
Preschool 10 students
TK-8 Mod/Severe 12 students
TK-8 Mod/Severe Autism Focus 10 students
TK-8 Mild/Mod 15 students
2

RSP
Each full-time RSP teacher will have an Instructional Assistant assigned to the resource program to
support students for 6 hours per school day.
Toileting
Teachers are responsible for instruction, supervision, and the learning of all students in the classroom.
When teachers step away to assist with toileting, it interrupts instruction and supervision for the entire
class. Trained support staff are better positioned to handle toileting needs so teachers can remain
focused on teaching, maintaining a safe classroom environment, and supporting student learning.
The District shall designate non-certificated personnel as the primary provider of student diapering and
other toileting needs. If support staff are unavailable, the site administrator, classroom teacher, or
other designee shall be responsible for contacting the parent/guardian to provide assistance.
Finally, requiring an analysis on multi-year projections in our school district budgets produces many
problems for union members and for the stability students need from districts. Instead of a tool to
support realistic budgeting, we see year after year LLCSD under projecting revenue and over
projecting certain expenses which inherently favor the employer in thwarting collective bargaining
demands, resulting in unnecessary threats of cuts, layoffs, increases to class sizes, and the
manufactured crisis we are now experiencing.
